Empirical Research Plan  
“Highways and Suburbanization, 1950-1990”

───────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
───────────────────────────────────────────
Primary strategy: Two-way fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension, instrumenting for potentially endogenous highway mileage with a plausibly exogenous historical plan (“IV-DID”).

Why it fits  
• The outcome (central-city vs. suburban population shares) is observed decennially for every metropolitan area from 1950 to 1990  panel structure.  
• Highway mileage within an MSA grows at different dates and intensities (“staggered adoption”).  
• Institutional context: the 1947 National Interregional Highway Plan laid out routes years before most construction and well before the suburban boom. That plan provides exogenous cross-sectional variation that predicts later highway placement but is uncorrelated with post-war suburbanization shocks, satisfying the relevance/exclusion conditions for an IV.  
• An event study around the first year of substantial highway penetration lets us visualize dynamic treatment effects and test pre-trends.

───────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
───────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
Treated_{mt} = cumulative miles of interstate highway in MSA m by decade t, scaled by MSA land area (miles / 100 square miles). A binary treatment version (HighExposure_{mt}) = 1 if miles per land-area exceeds the national median by decade t; 0 otherwise, is used for simple DID.

Instrument  
PlanMiles_{m} = miles of the 1947 planned interstate network falling inside MSA m (intersected with 1940 MSA boundaries), also scaled by land area.

Control group / counterfactual  
Metros with below-median (or zero) actual interstate mileage in a given decade serve as contemporaneous controls. With IV-DID, every metro enters both stages; causal identification comes from the exogenous component of mileage predicted by PlanMiles_{m}. We additionally run specifications where the 25 % of metros with the lowest eventual mileage are the permanent control group to guard against treatment contamination.

Treatment timing / event date  
Event time 0 for MSA m = first decade when cumulative interstate mileage > 10 miles (a threshold chosen because many metros get short “stubs” earlier). Leads k = –4 … –1 and lags k = 0 … +4 (i.e., 40 years) are included.

───────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
───────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends (conditional on FE & controls): In absence of highways, treated and control metros would have had similar changes in population distribution.  
Plausibility: Large-sample panel and event-study pre-trends can be inspected; pre-war (1930-1950) population trends can be added as controls.

A2. Exclusion (for IV): 1947 planned miles affect suburbanization only through realized post-1950 highways.  
Plausibility: Planning preceded modern suburban push; plan maps were drawn for military/commercial connectivity, not local land-use. We will show that PlanMiles is unrelated to pre-1950 urban decentralization or demographic attributes.

A3. First stage relevance: PlanMiles strongly predicts actual post-1950 mileage.  
Empirically testable; expected F-statistic >> 10.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): One metro’s highways do not directly change another metro’s internal population distribution (aside from general equilibrium effects).  
Plausibility: Reasonable at decadal/MBA scale; spillovers addressed by controlling for neighboring-metro mileage.

A5. No differential survivorship/compositional change of MSAs driven by treatment.  
We use constant 1990 MSA boundaries for all decades to prevent geographic reclassification bias.

───────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
───────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Endogenous route choice (highways built where suburban growth was already expected).  
• Use IV with 1947 plan.  
• Control for projected population in 1950, 1940 commuting patterns, and pre-war growth.  
• Event-study pre-trend test.

T2. Omitted policy shocks correlated with highways (e.g., local zoning, FHA mortgage guarantees).  
• Add decade×state FE to absorb state-level housing/finance policies.  
• Control for time-varying local fiscal variables (property tax rates, zoning changes where data permit).  
• Show robustness to adding WWII plant closures, Cold-War base openings, etc.

T3. Spillovers & migration across metro borders.  
• Include spatial lags of treatment (avg. highway miles in adjacent MSAs).  
• Show robustness to excluding the 20 MSAs whose borders are within 50 km of another large metro (“conjoined metros”).

───────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
───────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # twoway FE + IV
library(did2s)       # Callaway-Sant'Anna / Gardner
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------------------
census  <- fread("msa_population_1950_1990.csv")      # pop_cc, pop_suburb
highway <- fread("msa_highway_miles.csv")             # actual miles by decade
plan    <- fread("msa_1947_plan_miles.csv")           # planned miles
geo     <- fread("msa_geo_controls.csv")              # land area, topography
panel   <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by=c("msa","year"),all=TRUE),
                  list(census, highway, plan, geo))

# 2. Variable construction --------------------------------------------------
panel[, pop_share_suburb := pop_suburb / (pop_cc + pop_suburb)]
panel[, miles_area       := highway_miles / land_area_100]   # land_area_100 = 100 sq mi units
panel[, planned_density  := plan_miles / land_area_100]

# binary high-exposure indicator
q50 <- panel[year==1950, quantile(miles_area, 0.5, na.rm=TRUE)]
panel[, treat_bin := as.integer(miles_area > q50)]

# Event-time
first_mile <- panel[miles_area>0, .(first_year = min(year)), by=msa]
panel      <- merge(panel, first_mile, by="msa", all.x=TRUE)
panel[, event_time := year - first_year]         # NA for never-treated

# 3. Main IV-DID regression -------------------------------------------------
#   pop_share_suburb_{my} = β * miles_area_iv + δ_m + γ_t + X_{my}θ + ε
iv_main <- feols(pop_share_suburb ~ 1 | msa + year | 
                 miles_area ~ planned_density,
                 data = panel, cluster = ~msa)
summary(iv_main)

# 4. Event-study with Gardner (sun-abset) weights ---------------------------
es <- did2s(panel,
            yname   = "pop_share_suburb",
            first_stage  = ~ treat_bin,
            second_stage = ~ 0 | msa + year,
            treatment   = "treat_bin",
            idname  = "msa",
            tname   = "year")
# Plot ES coefficients
ggplot(es$dynamic_att, aes(event_time, att)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=att-1.96*se, ymax=att+1.96*se)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept= -1, lty=2) + theme_bw()

# 5. Robustness check: add state×decade FE ----------------------------------
panel[, state := substr(msa,1,2)]              # assume msa code embeds state
iv_state <- feols(pop_share_suburb ~ 1 | msa + factor(state)*year | 
                  miles_area ~ planned_density,
                  data = panel, cluster = ~msa)
etable(iv_main, iv_state)
```

───────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
───────────────────────────────────────────
Direction: Greater interstate mileage should raise the suburban share of population (β > 0) by lowering commuting costs from suburbs to CBDs.  

Back-of-the-envelope magnitude: A one-standard-deviation increase in highway density (~0.5 miles per 100 sq mi) might raise the suburban population share by 3–5 percentage points over 20 years (≈ 0.1 σ of the 1990 distribution).

───────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID/IV)
───────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Strong first stage (F-stat > 10) ............................... 1  
C2: Parallel pre-trends visually & statistically confirmed ......... 0.8  
C3: Exclusion of instrument (plausible, but debatable) ............. 0.7  
C4: No anticipation/SUTVA .......................................... 0.8  
C5: Robustness to alternative controls/specifications .............. 1  

Overall ≈ 0.86 → reasonably credible but still contingent on instrument validity and parallel pre-trends.
